entities.summary:
Liu Xin, courtesy name Zijun, was a Chinese astronomer, classicist, imperial librarian, mathematician, and politician during the Western Han and Xin dynasties. Born into the Liu family, which served as imperial librarians, Liu Xin was groomed for a life of scholarship and service from an early age. He became a prominent figure in the imperial court, serving as the chief astronomer and classicist for several emperors, including Emperor Ping of Han and Emperor Ai of Han.

Liu Xin's most significant contribution was his role in the compilation of the 'Huangdi Suanjing' (Yellow Emperor's Divination Classic), a foundational text of Chinese mathematics and astronomy. This work, completed around 14 BCE, marked a significant milestone in Chinese scientific inquiry and had a lasting impact on the development of mathematics and astronomy in East Asia.

Despite his many accomplishments, Liu Xin's life was marked by turmoil and personal struggle. In 23 CE, he died under mysterious circumstances, with some sources suggesting that he was poisoned by Emperor Ai's advisors. This event, combined with the naming taboo that forced him to change his name to Liu Xiu, has led some historians to speculate about the extent of Liu Xin's influence on the imperial court.

Liu Xin's legacy extends far beyond his own lifetime, however. His work on the 'Huangdi Suanjing' helped establish Chinese mathematics and astronomy as major disciplines, influencing scholars and scientists across Asia and beyond. Today, Liu Xin is recognized as a key figure in the development of Chinese science and culture, and his contributions continue to inspire new generations of scholars and researchers.

The 'Liu Xin Canon' of the 'Xiaoshu Jing'an' (Collection of Biographies of the Historians) records that Liu Xin was 'born in Luoyang' and 'died in Luoyang' at the age of 60. This brief yet poignant summary of his life and death serves as a powerful reminder of the enduring impact of Liu Xin's work and legacy.
